 WP(C) NO. 38102 OF 2016  2025:KER:39914  3
JUDGMENT
Petitioner's property in Pallippuram Village of Cherthala Taluk was acquired invoking the urgency clause under Section 17 of the Land Acquisition Act 1894.
Notification under Section 4(1) was published in Gazette dated 24.01.1997.
Declaration under Section 6 was issued on 27.07.1998 and was published in the Gazette dated 06.08.1998.

3. The writ petition was disposed of by this Court on 15.01.2015, judgment passed by this Court is extracted hereunder :-
"
The prayers 1 and 2 in the writ petition are in relation to Ext. P5 series awards passed as early as on 16.09.2000.
More than 14 years have elapsed by now and the challenge to the awards cannot be countenanced on the ground of delay.
2. The prayers 3 and 4 of the writ petition pertain to restoration of possession and ownership over the land which belonged to the petitioner.

The petitioner asserts that the respondents are not now in need of the land and has submitted Ext. P12 representation with the fourth respondent.
3. The petitioner is also free to submit a supplemental representation to the first respondent.
Any representation so filed within one month from today shall also be dealt with within one month therefrom.
The petitioner as well as the fourth respondent shall be put on notice and heard in the exercise.
The petitioner is free to urge her contentions and to ventilate her grievances."

The writ petition is disposed of No costs."
4.

This Court permitted the petitioner to submit a supplemental representation to the 1st respondent and directed that the same shall be considered after issuing notice to the petitioner as well as the requisitioning authority, Kerala State Industrial Development Corporation Ltd (KSIDC).

sentences.text: Pursuant to Ext.P6 judgment, the matter was considered by the Government.
Petitioner as well as the KSIDC were provided opportunity of hearing.
Ext.P7 order was passed on 08.01.2016, rejecting the request of the petitioner.

Petitioner thereafter approached this WP(C) NO. 38102 OF 2016 2025:KER:39914 Court in the above writ petition challenging Ext.P7 and seeking direction to the respondents to exclude the property of the petitioner from acquisition and to return the land.
5. Counter affidavit has been filed by the Government and a statement has been filed by the learned counsel appearing for the 4th respondent.

6. The learned counsel for the petitioner submitted that, the acquisition proceedings were under Section 17 of the Land Acquisition Act and various provisions of the Land Acquisition Act which are P.M.Fathima Barkath vs The State Of Kerala on 4 June, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/33843624/
3 mandatory in nature were violated.

sentences.text: He pointed out that, there was delay in passing the award and the said delay was attempted to be justified on the ground that some of the parties had approached this Court challenging the acquisition and 171 days time were required for the conclusion of the proceedings.

The Government in Ext.P7 has adopted a view that the time taken for completion of the proceedings before this Court, though was in writ petitions at the instance of others, can be taken into consideration in the case of all whose properties were proposed to be acquired under the same notification.

The learned Counsel submitted that the said view of the Government is erroneous as WP(C) NO. 38102 OF 2016 2025:KER:39914 the period can be excluded only with the respect of those properties with respect to which litigations were pending.
The learned Counsel for the petitioner invited my attention to paragraph no.4 of Ext.P7, wherein the specific contentions raised by the petitioner were enumerated by the Government.
He made specific reference to the 3rd contention noted by the Government which is regarding failure to pay 80% of the estimated compensation.
He also pointed out that specific argument was raised regarding the delay in passing of the award, as the same ought to have been passed before 05.08.2000, but was passed actually on 16.09.2000.
He also pointed out that the petitioner had a specific contention that the property was not utilized by the KSIDC and was remaining vacant.

He submitted that while passing Ext. P7 order,
Government failed to address the contentions of the petitioner in a proper perspective.
He submitted that, the question of delay was attempted to be addressed by an erroneous reason as noted above.
He pointed out that the specific contention regarding non-payment of 80% of estimate compensation was not at all addressed by the authority while passing Ext. P7.

He also pointed out that, the observations in Ext. P7, regarding the status WP(C) NO. 38102 OF 2016 2025:KER:39914 of the acquired land was only to the effect that the KSIDC had developed the land and was providing it to suitable industrial establishments.
He submitted that, at the time of issuing Ext. P7, no industries had actually been developed in the land acquired.

7. The learned Counsel for the petitioner made reference to the following judgments of the Hon'ble Supreme Court :-
(1) Delhi Airtech Services Pvt. Ltd and Others v. State of U.P and Others [2022 (4)
KLJ 854].
(2) Sukh Dutt Ratra v. State of Himachal Pradesh [2022 (7) SCC 508].
(3) Vidya Devi v. State of Himachal Pradesh and Others [2020 (2) SCC 569].

sentences.text: The obligation to pay compensation can also be inferred in Article 300A.

The Hon'ble Supreme Court has held that,
forcibly dispossessing a person of his private property without following due process of law, would be violative WP(C) NO. 38102 OF 2016 2025:KER:39914 of a human right, as also Constitutional right under Article 300A of the Constitution.
The learned Counsel made reference to the observation of the Hon'ble Supreme Court that, delay and laches cannot be raised in a case of a continuing cause of action.

Further, the learned Counsel pointed out that the Hon'ble Supreme Court observed that there is no period of limitation prescribed for the Courts to exercise their Constitutional jurisdiction to do substantial justice.

8. The learned Counsel contended specifically that, the acquisition in question is vitiated for failure to comply with the mandatory provisions of the Land Acquisition Act and those aspects were directed to be considered by the Government by this Court vide Ext. P6 judgment.
The learned Counsel argued that, the Government however failed to appreciate and analyze the legal contentions raised.
He therefore, submitted that Ext. P7 is vitiated by failure to consider relevant matters and also for taking into account of irrelevant considerations.
He submitted that, the land is liable to be restored to the petitioner as the acquisition is obviously not sustainable.

The learned Government Pleader, on the other hand, contended that, the petitioner is not entitled to maintain this writ petition, as in the earlier round of litigation, his contentions were considered and were not accepted by this Court.
The learned Government Pleader submitted that, this Court disposed of W.P.(C) No.33161 of 2014, filed by the petitioner after rejecting some of the reliefs sought.

The petitioner was permitted to submit a supplementary representation and the Government was directed to consider the same only for the reason that the petitioner submitted that, the land acquired was not then in need for the respondents.
He hence contended that, no relief is liable to be granted in this writ petition, as it is not at all maintainable.

Apart from challenging the maintainability of the writ petition, the learned Government Pleader cited the following judgments of the Hon'ble Supreme Court and also of this Court: -
(1) Huchamma (D) by L.Rs. v. State of Karnataka and Others [2009 (16) SCC 656].

sentences.text: The learned Government Pleader, relying on the above judgments contended that, belated challenges against land acquisition proceedings are not liable to be entertained.
He also submitted that, land once acquired cannot be re-conveyed or assigned to erstwhile owner and if the property was not required, then it should be sold in public auction.
The learned Government Pleader further submitted that, the acquired land was already utilized by the KSIDC by providing it to various industries.

He submitted that, now several industries are functioning in the acquired land and therefore, the claim of the petitioner for restoration of the property cannot be entertained in any view of the matter.
11. The learned Counsel appearing for the 4th respondent KSIDC pointed out the statement filed by him and submitted that, several industries have come up in the acquired land.
With reference to the statement, he submitted that six public sector industrial units and a private sector industrial unit is functioning in the acquired property.
He also submitted that, the highly belated challenge by the petitioner against the acquisition of the property cannot be entertained by this Court.

Having heard the learned Counsel appearing for the petitioner, the learned Government Pleader and the learned Counsel for the 4th respondent, I find that this Court by Ext. P6 judgment had provided an opportunity to the petitioner to raise her grievance before the Government.
It is true that, reliefs 1 and 2 sought in W.P.(C) No.33161 of 2014, were rejected by this Court on the ground of delay.

Those reliefs were with respect to the notification and declaration issued under the provisions of the Land Acquisition Act, as seen from the copy of the writ petition produced as Ext. R3(a) by the Government.
With respect to the reliefs 3 and 4 sought in W.P.(C) No.33161 of 2014, this Court did not express any opinion on merits, in Ext. P6 judgment.
Those reliefs were regarding restoration of possession and ownership and also for directing the respondents to take decision on the representation submitted by the petitioner.

Without expressing any opinion on those reliefs, this Court permitted the petitioner to submit a supplementary representation and directed the Government to consider the same with notice to the petitioner and also to the KSIDC.

Therefore,
question is as to whether the said exercise as directed by this Court was properly undertaken by the WP(C) NO. 38102 OF 2016 2025:KER:39914 Government.
As pointed out by the learned Counsel for the petitioner, contention raised by the petitioner were specifically noted by the Government in Ext. P7.

However, specific contention raised with regard to non-payment of 80% of the estimated compensation, which is a mandatory requirement under the Act, no discussion is available in Ext.
P7.
The issue was specifically noticed in paragraph no.4.

During the course of hearing the said alleged defect was highlighted by the learned Counsel for the petitioner and he also pointed out that,
inspite of a specific direction issued by this Court by way of interim order no clarification was given by the Government regarding payment of 80% of compensation.

He therefore, contended that non P.M.Fathima Barkath vs The State Of Kerala on 4 June, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/33843624/
6 consideration of said contention by the Government has caused serious prejudice to the petitioner.

sentences.text: 13. I do not want to express opinions on merits of the different contentions raised by both sides.

In view of the specific contentions of the learned Counsel for the petitioner of non- consideration of the contention of the petitioner regarding failure to pay 80% of the estimated compensation, I find it appropriate to set aside Ext. P7 order as it is vitiated by non-application of mind WP(C) NO. 38102 OF 2016 2025:KER:39914 to a germane contention.
Regarding the other aspects found against the petitioner by the Government and the merits of the same, this Court need not make any observations at this stage.
In view of the above discussion, I allow this writ petition, by setting aside Ext. P7 order.
The 1 st respondent shall consider the matter afresh after providing a another opportunity of hearing to the petitioner and also to the 4 th respondent KSIDC.
The petitioner and the KSIDC will be free to raise all available contentions.

The Government shall take a fresh decision in the matter after affording an opportunity of hearing as directed above, within a period of three months from the date of receipt of a copy of this judgment.

Other contentions raised and other reliefs sought in this writ petition are kept open.
Sd/-
S.MANU JUDGE ANK
